newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostages jog and diet to cope with captivity.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostages jog and diet to cope with captivity.

text.p: Hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima are dieting and jogging to lose weight, said a doctor and former captive on Friday who now treats the 72 men still held by Marxist rebels.

Heart specialist Miguel Sanchez Palacios told Peruvian television that on his latest visit on Thursday he found the hostages calm and in generally good health, despite 59 days in captivity at the hands of about 15 heavily-armed members of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).

"Although some of them go jogging on the second floor, because of the lack of physical exercise some have put on weight and have decided to go on a diet," said Dr. Sanchez Palacios, who was among the first batches of hostages to be released. "Some of them have lost 13 to 18 pounds (six to eight kg)."
"Looking at some of them, I'd say they look better for losing 18 pounds (eight kilos)," said the doctor.
One of the hostages, 55-year-old Deputy Energy and Mines Minister Jorge San Roman, recently wrote to his wife Martha to tell her he was glad to have trimmed his burly 220-pound (100- kg) frame.

The MRTA's Peruvian and Japanese captives have a daily choice of food from both countries supplied by the Red Cross, and are regularly sent baskets of fresh fruit by Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori's mother.

But, as the days and weeks go by, concern is growing for the physical and mental strain on the hostages, who include two government ministers, senior judges and security officials, the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia and Fujimori's brother and brother-in-law.

The Red Cross, which is also overseeing negotiations between the rebels and government that are expected to resume on Saturday, says hostages are being treated for hypertension, digestive problems and depression. It restored the power supply into the besieged house on Thursday to operate heart-monitoring equipment.
Two of the hostages, a Peruvian judge with arthritis and a member of Congress being treated for cancer, are particular causes of concern.
"But none of them is extremely ill," confirmed Dr. Sanchez Palacios.

He noted a sharp contrast between the "very tense atmosphere of terror" he felt in the first days of the siege, which began when the MRTA stormed the residence during a cocktail party on Dec. 17, and the "calm atmosphere, with a degree of camaraderie" that he felt on his latest visit.

"I'd like to reassure the hostages' families that from what I've seen they are in good health, the atmosphere is a lot calmer than at the start of this situation," said the doctor. "Alhough of course no one can be happy without his freedom."
